newsitem.title: UK: YEAREND - UK funds set to follow recovery sectors.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - UK funds set to follow recovery sectors.

text.p: Fund managers are ready to shape their British equities portfolios around the sectors which stand to gain most from a consumer-led economic recovery, a Reuters survey showed on Friday.

The poll of strategists and fund managers, conducted between December 3 and 10, showed that sectors benefiting from greater consumer prosperity such as retailing, housing and construction, were hot tips for 1997.
The experts were bearish about the banking sector, predicting a year of further consolidation and cut-throat competition, and also sounded a cautious tone about alcohol companies and utilities.
But they were largely in agreement that Britain would be in favour as a haven for investment during 1997.

"Broadly speaking, we would probably say domestic rather than international, manufacturing rather than consumer, maybe some mid-cap rather than (blue-chip)," said Ian Williams of Panmure Gordon, asked to pick his winning sectors for 1997.

"The sectors that we favour would be the cyclicals, industrial stocks. They have been hurt very badly in the last few months," said Ian Scott, European equities strategist with Lehman Brothers in London.
With the British property market widely predicted to be ready for a hectic 1997, fund managers said they were ready to cash in on rising prices.
"The economy is growing quite quickly at the moment and that should lead to rising rents and asset values," said Michael Ashbridge, investment director at Save and Prosper.
And David Binnie, UK fund manager at Scottish Life, said the building materials sector would be in for a good year.
Binnie pointed out that investing by sector was nowadays a risky venture.

"We are much more company specific. There are a lot of good quality companies there, we have stuck mostly to the better quality names, companies which are going to give you a good performance over the longer run," he said.
Binnie sounded a warning against utility companies and alcohol firms, both recent favourites.

"We are avoiding alcoholic beverages and utilities -- electricity, gas and water and to a lesser extent telecoms. These companies will produce below average earnings growth," he said. He cited various micro and macro-economic factors afflicting drinks companies, and added that he was not particularly impressed with the quality of management.
Britain's ageing population would continue to benefit pharmaceuticals and health care firms, analysts said.

"We think pharmaceuticals are a genuine growth sector...We are also very keen on life assurance because just as in other countries, the demographic trend means that people have to save much more for their future welfare," said Ashbridge.
Britain's impending general election, which is widely expected to put the opposition Labour party into power, was seen as a relatively minor, delaying factor in investment plans.

"Overseas institutions are wary ahead of an election, so it's difficult to see the market making a huge amount of progress ahead of a likely election in May," said Gary Dugan, European equities market strategist with JP Morgan.
Panmure Gordon's Williams said he was quite keen on the manufacturing sector.
"But the difficulty these days is that the actual domestic manufacturing sector in stock market terms is absolutely tiny."

"It is very difficult to know what stocks to buy on that basis because many of the traditional manufacturing sectors have shrunk quite dramatically as a result of long-term underperformance. And a lot of the big companies in those areas have pretty big overseas exposure," he said.
Richard Jeffrey, Group Economist at Charterhouse, also gave his blessing to manufacturers.
"I think, with strengthening UK growth particularly in the industrial sector, that manufacturing will regain some of its lost ground and probably lead the way," he said.
"But I wouldn't ignore the consumer stocks, because they are also going to benefit from very strong consumer spending."

Jeffrey was one of several experts who said he was nervous about the banking sector owing to continuing consolidation in the field, and added that he suspected oil companies would not perform in 1997 as well as they had done this year.
